newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Cod, an epic fish story with a tragic end.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cod, an epic fish story with a tragic end.

text.p: Cod is eaten in a thousand ways from the Arctic Circle to Africa, but until author Mark Kurlansky came along no one celebrated it as the tragic fish that changed the world.

Like a detective stumbling on clues, Kurlansky, a food columnist, journalist and author of books on the Caribbean and postwar European Jewry, found that his reporting over the years and around the world included a common theme: cod.

Vikings filled their bellies with it when they terrorised Europe and sailed to North America. Slaves in the West Indies lived on high-protein salted cod. New England fishermen made themselves into a wealthy "codfish aristocracy." And even today, as the cod struggles to survive, Nigerians relish the delicate flesh from cured cod's head.

"It's a classic tragedy -- a fish achieves greatness, fame, renown around the world, only to be destroyed by its flaws," said Kurlansky, author of the just-published "Cod: A Biography of the Fish That Changed the World" (Walker & Co.).

Kurlansky, 48, who grew up in Hartford, Connecticut, worked during college as a fisherman in cod-crazy New England. With the burly build of a deckhand and a ruddy round face topped by a tangle of salt-and-pepper hair, he could blend easily with the grizzled cod fishermen who still shove off before dawn into icy coastal waters.

But in New York, where he now lives, Kurlansky fits in just as well at a fashionable French restaurant as he explains the fine points of a dish of cod cheeks Provencal. "The cheeks are rarely served with this side bone," he said, forking out the disk of milky white flesh. "I think they got this from a salted dried head, which is a fairly new thing. Nigerians -- Nigerians love salted dried head."
TALKING TILL THE COD COMES HOME

Get him started, in fact, and Kurlansky can talk until the cod come home. His book, larded with recipes old and new, gee-whiz tidbits and tales of cod wars, ecological devastation and sea stories galore, has had a warm reception from critics.

The New York Times' Christopher Lehmann-Haupt praised its "quirky take on human history." Andrew Nikiforuk, in Toronto's Globe and Mail, called the book "eloquent, learned and full of earthy narratives that delight and appall."

The teeming fisheries off North America and its rocky coasts, ideal for drying fish, drew English, Spanish, Basque and Portuguese fishermen and spurred the settlement of the New World. By the middle of the 16th century and for another 200 years, 60 percent of the fish eaten in Europe was cod.

The durable bottom-dweller was once defined as "a species of fish too well known to require any description." Britain's famed fish and chips was made from cod, a wooden carving of the fish hangs in the Massachusetts state legislature, and in Spanish "one who cuts the salt cod" is the person in charge.

Dried cod loses four-fifths of its original weight through evaporation, has almost no fat and is 80 percent protein. Nearly everything on a cod can be eaten including the skin, stomach, eggs, throat, air bladder, gonads, the delicate cheeks and, of course, awful-tasting cod liver oil. Icelanders up until this century even softened the bones in sour milk and ate them in a kind of gruel, Kurlansky said.
COD, A CAUSE OF THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION

Dried and salted cod was a mainstay of New England's trade with Africa and the slave plantations of the West Indies. Kurlansky contends that control of Caribbean commerce and cod fishing were among the causes of the American Revolution.

Back then, the rich fishing grounds of the North Atlantic seemed inexhaustible, but the coming of engine-powered boats and bigger nets and refrigeration have brought cod to the vanishing point. With man as its major predator, cod were "at the wrong end of a 1,000-year fishing spree," Kurlansky wrote.

Cod's nature fated it to be a tragic candidate for extinction. "It's easy to catch, it'll eat anything, it moves inshore to spawn, it likes shallow water." As a result, Kurlansky said, "It faces total destruction."
The United States and Canada restricted Atlantic fishing to try to revive stocks, although Canada announced this spring it would allow some commercial cod harvesting.

Kurlansky said fish were the last food still caught in the wild and the cod's story raised disturbing questions about whether man and wild creatures could co-exist. Referring to the downtrodden hero of Arthur Miller's play "Death of a Salesman," he called cod "the Willy Loman of fish, the out-of-fashion fish ... feeding the common people, not making it into restaurants like this until it was nearly extinct."
He added, "It's suddenly chic to eat the last cod. Or maybe we can't appreciate food until it becomes rare."
